issues.legal_issue: A widow’s adoption of her daughter’s son is valid when the relevant community custom and the fact of adoption are established by the evidence.
material_facts: The widow adopted her daughter’s son after her husband’s death.
The courts below found the adoption valid under the community custom and established as a fact.
The Supreme Court found ample evidentiary support for both findings.
issues.conclusion: The adoption was true and valid, both as a matter of custom and fact.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated custom as a source of Hindu law and upheld the concurrent findings where the evidence adequately established the custom and the factum of adoption. It relied on the evidence in the record and did not disturb the lower courts’ factual findings.

predicates.adoption_validity_appeal: The proceeding challenges the validity of an adoption recognized by the courts below.
predicates.customary_adoption_supported: The evidence supports the existence of a custom permitting the adoption in question.
predicates.adoption_fact_supported: The evidence supports that the adoption actually took place.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenging an adoption is supported by evidence establishing the relevant custom or the fact of adoption, the adoption is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A valid adoption by a coparcener’s widow permits the adopted son to claim a share despite an intervening partition, but does not undo the separation of the family.
material_facts: The adoptive father died while the family was governed by Mitakshara law and the family property was coparcenary property.
A partition between the remaining coparceners took place after the adoptive father’s death and before the widow adopted the plaintiff.
The adopted son sought a share by reopening the earlier partition.
issues.conclusion: The adopted son could claim a share as if he had been alive when his adoptive father died, but the later adoption did not wipe out the fact of partition or reunite the divided family.
issues.legal_principle: Under the pre-statutory Mitakshara law of adoption, the doctrine of relation back allowed the adopted son to claim a share as if he had been begotten and alive when the adoptive father died. The fiction did not erase the actual division of status or restore the family to jointness. The court relied particularly on Govind v. Nagappa, and also considered P. Ammal v. Ramalingam, Srinivas, Krishnamurthi, and the other authorities discussed in the judgment. It noted that section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 altered the prior-law setting and that section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 makes the adopted child the child of the adoptive parent from the date of adoption; the present dispute concerned a pre-statutory adoption.

predicates.adopted_son_partition_claim: An adopted son seeks a share of coparcenary property by challenging a partition made before his adoption.
predicates.valid_widow_adoption: A widow validly adopts a son to her deceased coparcener husband.
predicates.prior_coparcenary_partition: The coparcenary was partitioned after the adoptive father’s death and before the adoption.

issues.definition: When a validly adopted son seeks a share after an intervening coparcenary partition, he can claim a share without restoring the family to joint status.

issues.legal_issue: A lawful transfer of a coparcener’s separate share made before a widow’s later adoption is not subject to challenge by the adopted son.
material_facts: A partition had allotted a separate share to one coparcener.
After the partition, that coparcener gifted his entire allotted share to his grandson before the adoption occurred.
The court found that the donor could transfer the share allotted to him and that the gift was lawful.
issues.conclusion: The gift was immune from challenge by the subsequently adopted son, and the gifted property was excluded when calculating the available property for his share.
issues.legal_principle: The relation-back doctrine does not invalidate a disposition lawfully made before the adoption. A member of a Mitakshara family may freely transfer a share validly allotted to him at partition where his own issue have no birthright in it. The court relied on Govind v. Nagappa, Bhimji Krishna Rao, Bijoor v. Padmanabh, Krishtappa v. Gopal, and the other authorities discussed in the judgment. It distinguished transfers by persons with limited powers, including a widow, which bind an adopted son only if the applicable Hindu-law conditions are met.

rule.if: adopted_son_challenges_prior_transfer and valid_prior_partition and transferor_had_power_over_separate_share and transfer_made_before_adoption

predicates.adopted_son_challenges_prior_transfer: An adopted son challenges a transfer made before his adoption.
predicates.valid_prior_partition: The property had been validly allotted to the transferor in a partition.
predicates.transferor_had_power_over_separate_share: The transferor had legal power to dispose of the separately allotted property.
predicates.transfer_made_before_adoption: The transfer occurred before the widow adopted the son.

issues.definition: A transfer made before adoption binds the adopted son when it concerns property validly allotted to a transferor who had power to dispose of it.

issues.legal_issue: A share claimed after a prior partition must be worked out equitably against the property remaining with the branch from which it can be recovered.
material_facts: The adopted son’s share was assessed by reference to the family property at the time of the earlier partition.
One coparcener’s entire allotted share had been validly gifted away before the adoption.
The other coparcener’s allotted properties remained with his branch at the time of adoption.
An allotment had been set aside for the adoptive mother’s residence and maintenance.

The court considered it unfair both to confine the adopted son to a fraction of the remaining properties and to make the remaining branch bear the full burden of the share calculated on the original estate.
issues.conclusion: The adopted son was awarded one half of the properties allotted to the remaining branch at the earlier partition that were still with that branch at the date of adoption, including the maintenance allotment. Profits were payable on that basis, and maintenance payable by that branch to the adoptive mother was to cease.
issues.legal_principle: When an earlier partition is reopened to give an adopted son his share, the share must be worked out fairly and equitably in light of intervening proprietary events. Property validly transferred before adoption is excluded from the available corpus, while the maintenance allotment was brought into the corpus. The court followed the equitable approach in Krishtappa v. Gopal and applied the relation-back and transfer principles discussed in Govind v. Nagappa and the other cited authorities.

rule.if: adopted_son_seeks_partition_share and prior_valid_partition and one_branch_share_transferred_before_adoption and other_branch_property_remained_at_adoption and maintenance_property_set_aside

predicates.adopted_son_seeks_partition_share: An adopted son seeks a share of family property after an earlier partition.
predicates.prior_valid_partition: The family property was validly divided before the adoption.
predicates.one_branch_share_transferred_before_adop: A branch’s allotted share was validly transferred before the adoption.
predicates.other_branch_property_remained_at_adopti: Property allotted to another branch remained with that branch when the adoption occurred.
predicates.maintenance_property_set_aside: Property had been set aside for the adoptive mother’s residence or maintenance.

issues.definition: When an adopted son seeks a share after a valid partition, one branch’s share has been transferred before adoption, and property remains with another branch, he receives half of that remaining property, with the maintenance allotment included where applicable.
